claim: Mutations in Park8, encoding for the multidomain Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) protein, comprise the predominant genetic cause of Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Mutations in Park8, encoding for the multidomain Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) protein, comprise the predominant genetic cause of Parkinson's disease (PD).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about LRRK2 mutations and their role in Parkinson's disease.

claim: G2019S, the most common amino acid substitution in LRRK2, activates the kinase two- to threefold.
source: G2019S, the most common amino acid substitution activates the kinase two- to threefold.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: LRRK2 directly phosphorylates a subset of Rab GTPases both in vivo and in vitro on an evolutionary conserved residue in the switch II domain.
source: LRRK2 directly phosphorylates these both in vivo and in vitro on an evolutionary conserved residue in the switch II domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro kinase assays and in vivo phosphoproteomics experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pathogenic LRRK2 variants mapping to different functional domains increase phosphorylation of Rabs.
source: Pathogenic LRRK2 variants mapping to different functional domains increase phosphorylation of Rabs and this strongly decreases their affinity to regulatory proteins including Rab GDP dissociation inhibitors (GDIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased Rab phosphorylation with different LRRK2 mutations.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rabs by LRRK2 strongly decreases their affinity to regulatory proteins including Rab GDP dissociation inhibitors (GDIs).
source: Pathogenic LRRK2 variants mapping to different functional domains increase phosphorylation of Rabs and this strongly decreases their affinity to regulatory proteins including Rab GDP dissociation inhibitors (GDIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity-purification mass spectrometry and biochemical assays showing decreased GDI binding to phosphorylated Rabs.

claim: Parkinson's disease affects 1–2% of the elderly population.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting 1–2% of the elderly population (Lees et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lees et al., 2009.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have related 28 genetic risk variants at 24 loci with nonfamilial PD.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have related 28 genetic risk variants at 24 loci with nonfamilial PD (Nalls et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nalls et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations in LRRK2 (Park8) are found in hereditary forms of PD.
source: Among those, mutations in LRRK2 (Park8) are also found in hereditary forms, pinpointing a shared molecular pathway driving pathogenesis in both familial and non-familial PD and comprising the most common cause of the disease (Simón-Sánchez et al., 2009; Satake et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simón-Sánchez et al., 2009 and Satake et al., 2009.

claim: PD pathogenic LRRK2 mutations map predominantly to the kinase (G2019S, I2020T) and the ROC-COR domains (R1441C/G/H, Y1699C).
source: PD pathogenic LRRK2 mutations map predominantly to the kinase (G2019S, I2020T) and the ROC-COR domains (R1441C/G/H, Y1699C), implying that these enzymatic activities are crucial for pathogenesis (Rudenko and Cookson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rudenko and Cookson, 2014.

claim: The most common PD-associated LRRK2 mutation is the G2019S amino acid substitution, which activates the kinase two- to threefold.
source: The most common PD-associated LRRK2 mutation is the G2019S amino acid substitution, which activates the kinase two- to threefold (West et al., 2005; Khan, 2005; Jaleel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to West et al., 2005; Khan, 2005; and Jaleel et al., 2007.

claim: LRRK2 has been associated with diverse cellular processes such as Wnt signaling, mitochondrial disease, cytoskeleton remodeling, vesicular trafficking, autophagy, and protein translation.
source: Extensive studies of LRRK2 have associated it with diverse cellular processes such as Wnt signaling, mitochondrial disease, cytoskeleton remodeling, vesicular trafficking, autophagy, and protein translation (Taymans et al., 2015; Cookson, 2015; Schapansky et al., 2014; Papkovskaia et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taymans et al., 2015; Cookson, 2015; Schapansky et al., 2014; and Papkovskaia et al., 2012.

claim: Evidence that previously reported LRRK2 substrates are phosphorylated by LRRK2 in a physiological context is generally lacking.
source: Moreover, several LRRK2 substrates have been reported previously; however, evidence that they are phosphorylated by LRRK2 in a physiological context is generally lacking and proofs are confined to in vitro approaches or to cellular systems using overexpressed kinase (Jaleel et al., 2007; Kumar et al., 2010; Ohta et al., 2011; Kawakami et al., 2012; Bailey et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2014; Qing et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012; Gloeckner et al., 2009; Imai et al., 2008; Gillardon, 2009; Kanao et al., 2010; Matta et al., 2012; Xiong et al., 2012; Yun et al., 2013; Yun et al., 2015; Krumova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and represents a critical assessment of the existing literature.

claim: Depletion of Rab7L1 recapitulates the dopaminergic neuron loss observed with LRRK2-G2019S expression.
source: Depletion of Rab7L1 recapitulates the dopaminergic neuron loss observed with LRRK2-G2019S expression and its overexpression rescues mutant LRRK2 phenotypes (MacLeod et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacLeod et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of Rab7L1 rescues mutant LRRK2 phenotypes.
source: Depletion of Rab7L1 recapitulates the dopaminergic neuron loss observed with LRRK2-G2019S expression and its overexpression rescues mutant LRRK2 phenotypes (MacLeod et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to MacLeod et al., 2013.

claim: Rab GTPases comprise ~70 family members in humans.
source: Rab GTPases comprise ~70 family members in humans, and they are key players in all forms of intracellular vesicular trafficking events (Stenmark, 2009; Rivero-Ríos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stenmark, 2009 and Rivero-Ríos et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in Rab39b (Park21 locus) predispose to PD in humans.
source: For example, mutations in Rab39b (Park21 locus) predispose to PD in humans (Wilson et al., 2014; Mata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2014 and Mata et al., 2015.

claim: Overexpression of Rab8a, Rab1, and Rab3a attenuate α-synclein-induced cytotoxicity in cellular and animal models of PD.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Rab8a, Rab1, and Rab3a attenuate α-synclein-induced cytotoxicity in cellular and animal models of PD, suggesting a functional interplay between Rab GTPases and known PD factors (Cooper, 2006; Gitler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cooper, 2006 and Gitler et al., 2008.

claim: PINK1 has been reported to indirectly control the phosphorylation of a small group of Rabs including Rab8a at Ser111.
source: Recently, another PD-connected protein kinase termed PTEN-Induce Kinase-1 (PINK1) has been reported to indirectly control the phosphorylation of a small group of Rabs including Rab8a at Ser111 (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lai et al., 2015.

claim: Only pS935-LRRK2 and T73-Rab10 passed the stringent filtering criteria of overlapping both phosphoproteomic screens.
source: Remarkably, only two phosphosites passed these stringent filtering criteria, our positive control pS935-LRRK2 and the conserved T73 residue of the small GTPase Rab10 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the two phosphoproteomic screens and is shown in Figure 1H.

claim: T73 of Rab10 is located in the switch II domain.
source: The T73 residue of Rab10 is located in the switch II domain, which is characteristic of Rab GTPases (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The equivalent site to T73-Rab10 is highly conserved in more than 40 human Rab-family members.
source: Sequence alignment revealed that the equivalent site to T73-Rab10 is highly conserved in more than 40 human Rab-family members, indicating strong functional relevance (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both wt and LRRK2-G2019S, but neither kinase inactive D1994A mutant nor small molecule-inhibited LRRK2, efficiently phosphorylated Rab10.
source: Notably, we found that both wt and LRRK2-G2019S, but neither kinase inactive D1994A mutant nor small molecule-inhibited LRRK2, efficiently phosphorylated Rab10, proving a direct kinase-substrate relationship (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Incubation of Rab10 with LRRK2 followed by tryptic digestion and MS analysis unambiguously identified T73 as the major phosphorylation site.
source: Furthermore, incubation of Rab10 with LRRK2 followed by tryptic digestion and MS analysis unambiguously identified T73 as the major phosphorylation site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LRRK2 phosphorylates Rab8a, Rab1a, and Rab1b on the predicted LRRK2 phosphorylation site in the switch II domain.
source: Remarkably, all proteins were rapidly phosphorylated on the predicted LRRK2 phosphorylation site in the switch II domain (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry and Edman sequencing data shown in Figures 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Rabs with threonines (Rab1b, Rab8a, and Rab10) were efficiently phosphorylated by LRRK2, while those with the equivalent serine sites (Rab5b, Rab7a, Rab7L1, Rab12, and Rab39b) were phosphorylated to a drastically lower extent.
source: Interestingly, while Rabs with threonines (Rab1b, Rab8a, and Rab10) were efficiently phosphorylated, those with the equivalent serine sites (Rab5b, Rab7a, Rab7L1, Rab12, and Rab39b) were phosphorylated to a drastically lower extent (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Phosphorylation levels of Rab8a were about ten times higher compared to Rps15 and Msn.
source: Strikingly, levels of pRab8a were about ten times higher as compared to Rps15 and Msn, two of the best in vitro LRRK2 substrates known to date, demonstrating that Rabs with Thr sites in the switch II domain are primary LRRK2 targets (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: pS105-Rab12 was among the significantly modulated sites in PS1 and also downregulated upon MLI-2 treatment in wt cells as compared to the inhibitor-resistant A2016T mutant in PS2.
source: Surprisingly, we noticed that pS105-Rab12, which is not phosphorylated by LRRK2 in vitro (Figure 2G), was among the significantly modulated sites in PS1 and also downregulated upon MLI-2 treatment in wt cells as compared to the inhibitor-resistant A2016T mutant in PS2 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: T73-Rab10 is conserved in C. elegans and D. melanogaster.
source: LRRK2 kinase is conserved also in flies and worms and this is true of the T73-Rab10 substrate site as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S105-Rab12 is present throughout the vertebrates.
source: Also, S105-Rab12 is present throughout the vertebrates (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Total protein levels of Rab10 and Rab12 did not change appreciably in the A2016T knock-in model.
source: Total protein levels of Rab10 and Rab12 did not change appreciably in the A2016T knock-in model as judged by quantitative MS analysis, ruling out that that the observed phospho-level changes are due to differential protein expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: T86-Rab3a is clearly a LRRK2 target.
source: Whereas T86-Rab3a is clearly a LRRK2 target, Rab1a is not, indicating that overexpression of LRRK2 is not sufficient to phosphorylate all Rabs in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Overexpression of LRRK2 is not sufficient to phosphorylate Rab1a in cells.
source: Whereas T86-Rab3a is clearly a LRRK2 target, Rab1a is not, indicating that overexpression of LRRK2 is not sufficient to phosphorylate all Rabs in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In LRRK2 knockout MEFs, the decrease in pT72-Rab8 and pT73-Rab10 was only about twofold compared to wt, implying a very low intrinsic LRRK2 activity in cells.
source: In the knock-out, the decrease was only about twofold compared to wt, implying a very low intrinsic LRRK2 activity in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative MS analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F-I and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Quantitative MS analysis revealed a threefold increase in both pT72-Rab8 and pT73-Rab10 in LRRK2-G2019SGSK MEFs compared to wt.
source: Consistent with the two- to threefold increased in vitro activity of MEFs-extracted LRRK2-G2019SGSK (Figure 1B), our quantitative MS analysis revealed a threefold increase in both pT72-Rab8 and pT73-Rab10, which was restored to near wt levels by selective LRRK2 kinase inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative MS analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F-I.

claim: Levels of pT72-Rab8 and pS105-Rab12 were decreased more than twofold upon LRRK2 inhibition in LRRK2-G2019SLilly mouse brain.
source: Levels of pT72-Rab8 and pS105-Rab12 were decreased more than twofold upon LRRK2 inhibition, validating our findings in the context of a LRRK2 pathogenic mouse model (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from mouse brain shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Transiently expressed epitope-tagged LRRK2 and Rab8a efficiently associated with each other.
source: Indeed, affinity-purification mass-spectrometry (AP-MS) showed that transiently expressed epitope-tagged LRRK2 and Rab8a efficiently associated with each other, demonstrating that LRRK2 is able to form stable complexes with Rab GTPases in cells (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity-purification mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Rab10 and Rab12 associate with LRRK2 when transiently overexpressed in HEK293 cells.
source: Similarly, Rab10 as well as Rab12 associate with LRRK2 when transiently overexpressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity-purification mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: PD-associated mutations located in the kinase domain that augment LRRK2 kinase activity increase pT72-Rab8a and pT73-Rab10 levels in cells.
source: This revealed that besides PD-associated mutations located in the kinase domain that augment LRRK2 kinase activity, those occurring in the GTPase (ROC-COR) or the WD-40 domains also increased pT72-Rab8a and pT73-Rab10 levels in cells (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: PD-associated mutations occurring in the GTPase (ROC-COR) or the WD-40 domains increase pT72-Rab8a and pT73-Rab10 levels in cells.
source: This revealed that besides PD-associated mutations located in the kinase domain that augment LRRK2 kinase activity, those occurring in the GTPase (ROC-COR) or the WD-40 domains also increased pT72-Rab8a and pT73-Rab10 levels in cells (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: The G2019S mutation resulted in a two- to threefold increase in Rab8a phosphorylation in vitro compared to wt.
source: As expected, compared to wt, the G2019S mutation resulted in a two- to threefold increase in Rab8a phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: The ROC-COR domain R1441C mutation failed to increase Rab8a phosphorylation in vitro.
source: However, the ROC-COR domain R1441C mutation failed to do so, which is consistent with previous data suggesting that these mutations do not directly enhance LRRK2 kinase activity (Nichols et al., 2010), indicating that its effect on Rab8a phosphorylation levels is mediated by accessory factors in cells (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figures 4F and 4G and a citation to Nichols et al., 2010.

claim: The effect of the R1441C mutation on Rab8a phosphorylation levels is mediated by accessory factors in cells.
source: However, the ROC-COR domain R1441C mutation failed to do so, which is consistent with previous data suggesting that these mutations do not directly enhance LRRK2 kinase activity (Nichols et al., 2010), indicating that its effect on Rab8a phosphorylation levels is mediated by accessory factors in cells (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that R1441C increases Rab8a phosphorylation in cells but not in vitro.

claim: The LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation site is in the switch II region of Rab8a.
source: In the crystal structure of Rab8a (Guo et al., 2013), the LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation site is in the switch II region (Figure 2A), which regulates hydrolysis of GTP and coordinates the binding to various regulatory proteins (Pfeffer, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A and citations to Guo et al., 2013 and Pfeffer, 2005.

claim: Binding affinities of wt and the T72E mutant Rab8a for GDP and GMPPNP did not differ.
source: Binding affinities of wt and the TE mutant, determined with fluorescently labeled (N-Methylanthraniloyl, mant) GDP and non-hydrolysable GTP analogue GMPPNP, did not differ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A number of proteins preferentially bind to non-phosphorylatable T72A-Rab8a compared to the T72E phosphomimetic protein.
source: In contrast, AP-MS revealed that a number of proteins preferentially bind to non-phosphorylatable T72A-Rab8a compared to the T72E phosphomimetic protein (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity-purification mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Proteins that preferentially bind to T72A-Rab8a include Rab GDP dissociation inhibitors α and β (GDI1 and GDI2), Rab geranyltransferase complex members (CHM, CHML, and RabGGTA/RabGGTB), the Rab8a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Rabin8 (Rab3IP), a guanine nucleotide activating protein TBC1D15 and the inositol phosphatase INPP5B.
source: These were Rab GDP dissociation inhibitors α and β (GDI1 and GDI2), Rab geranyltransferase complex members (CHM, CHML, and RabGGTA/RabGGTB), the Rab8a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Rabin8 (Rab3IP), a guanine nucleotide activating protein TBC1D15 and the inositol phosphatase INPP5B (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity-purification mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The T72E phosphomimetic substitution decreased the level of Rabin8-catalyzed mant-GDP displacement from a Rab8-GDP complex compared to wt.
source: We found that compared to wt, the T72E phosphomimetic substitution decreased the level of Rabin8-catalyzed mant-GDP displacement from a Rab8-GDP complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence-based GEF assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: LRRK2-induced phosphorylation of T72-Rab8a inhibits rates of Rabin8-catalyzed GDP exchange fourfold.
source: Loading of non-phosphorylated and phosphorylated Rab8a with mant-GDP following incubation with Rabin8 revealed that LRRK2-induced phosphorylation of T72-Rab8a inhibits rates of Rabin8-catalyzed GDP exchange fourfold and decreases Rab8a-Rabin8 interaction (Figures 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence-based GEF assay data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: LRRK2-induced phosphorylation of T72-Rab8a decreases Rab8a-Rabin8 interaction.
source: Loading of non-phosphorylated and phosphorylated Rab8a with mant-GDP following incubation with Rabin8 revealed that LRRK2-induced phosphorylation of T72-Rab8a inhibits rates of Rabin8-catalyzed GDP exchange fourfold and decreases Rab8a-Rabin8 interaction (Figures 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ni2+-NTA pull-down data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Both λ-phosphatase treatment of LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab8a and pharmacological inhibition of LRRK2 prevented the decreased GEF activity of Rabin8 toward pT72-Rab8a.
source: Both λ-phosphatase treatment of LRRK2-phosphorylated Rab8a and pharmacological inhibition of LRRK2 prevented the decreased GEF activity of Rabin8 toward pT72-Rab8a (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence-based GEF assay data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rab8a by LRRK2 can limit its activation by Rabin8.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Rab8a by LRRK2 can limit its activation by Rabin8.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation decreases Rabin8 GEF activity toward Rab8a.

claim: Neither S106E-Rab12 nor T73E-Rab10 was able to bind GDIs, as compared to non-phosphorylatable Rab10 and Rab12.
source: As compared to non-phosphorylatable Rab10 and Rab12, neither S106E-Rab12 nor T73E-Rab10 was able to bind GDIs, demonstrating the functional importance of these residues (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 6A, 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The level of Rab8a-GDI interaction closely correlated with the degree of T72-Rab8a phosphorylation.
source: Strikingly, the level of Rab8a-GDI interaction closely correlated with the degree of T72-Rab8a phosphorylation (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation of S106-Rab12 diminished the interaction with GDIs.
source: Similarly, LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation of S106-Rab12 diminished the interaction with GDIs, confirming that the effect is not specific to one Rab isoform (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: All tested LRRK2 pathogenic mutations that affect kinase activity control the interaction of Rabs with GDIs.
source: All tested LRRK2 pathogenic mutations that affect kinase activity thus control the interaction of Rabs with GDIs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that different LRRK2 pathogenic mutations increase Rab phosphorylation and decrease GDI binding.

claim: There is a twofold increase of non-phosphorylatable T72A mutant Rab8 in the cytosol compared to T72E.
source: This revealed a twofold increase of non-phosphorylatable T72A mutant in the cytosol.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC-based subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: There is a significant increase of T72E-Rab8 protein levels in the membrane fraction compared to T72A.
source: Consistently, we detected a significant (p= 2.58*10-3) increase of T72E-Rab8 protein levels in the membrane fraction, demonstrating that interference with the Rab-GDI interaction results in an unbalanced membrane-cytosol distribution of Rabs (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC-based subcellular fractionation data shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: Interference with the Rab-GDI interaction results in an unbalanced membrane-cytosol distribution of Rabs.
source: Consistently, we detected a significant (p= 2.58*10-3) increase of T72E-Rab8 protein levels in the membrane fraction, demonstrating that interference with the Rab-GDI interaction results in an unbalanced membrane-cytosol distribution of Rabs (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the SILAC-based subcellular fractionation data showing differential distribution of T72A and T72E Rab8.

claim: LRRK2-/- mice and rats have deformed kidneys and lungs, indicative of defects in the autophagosome/lysosome pathway.
source: LRRK2-/- mice and rats have deformed kidneys and lungs, indicative of defects in the autophagosome/lysosome pathway, which depend on properly tuned Rab activity (Herzig et al., 2011; Hinkle et al., 2012; Baptista et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herzig et al., 2011; Hinkle et al., 2012; and Baptista et al., 2013.

claim: LRRK2 and Rab2a regulate Paneth cell function, which is compromised in Crohn's disease.
source: Moreover, it was recently reported that LRRK2 and Rab2a regulate Paneth cell function, which is compromised in Crohn's disease (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: LRRK2 induces phosphorylation of Rabs and deregulates cycling between cytosol and target membrane compartments.
source: In conclusion, we prove that LRRK2 induces phosphorylation of Rabs and provide evidence that it deregulates cycling between cytosol and target membrane compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Discovery of a key physiological LRRK2 substrate should inform and accelerate research into PD, including monitoring the efficacy of therapeutic intervention.
source: Discovery of a key physiological LRRK2 substrate should inform and accelerate research into PD, including monitoring the efficacy of therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: The A2016T substitution does not change basal LRRK2 activity but decreases sensitivity to MLI-2 ~10-fold.
source: The A2016T substitution does not change basal LRRK2 activity but decreases sensitivity to MLI-2 ~10-fold (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figures 1C, 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At a dose of 10 nM MLI-2, there was a substantial decrease in phosphorylation of LRRK2-pS935 in wt but not in A2016T cells.
source: At a dose of 10 nM, we observed a substantial decrease in phosphorylation of LRRK2-pS935, which is associated with LRRK2 kinase activity (Dzamko et al., 2010), in wt but not in A2016T cells (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and a citation to Dzamko et al., 2010.

claim: Over 9000 high-confidence phosphosites were quantified in each replicate in both screens.
source: Using a state-of-the-art workflow for phosphopeptide enrichment, label-free LC-MS/MS and the MaxQuant environment for stringent statistical data evaluation (Humphrey et al., 2015; Cox and Mann, 2008; Cox et al., 2011), we quantified over 9000 high-confidence phosphosites in each replicate in both screens (median R=0.80 and 0.89 in PS1 and PS2, respectively), (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In PS1, 234 sites were significantly regulated after treatment with each of the two LRRK2 compounds GSK2578215A and HG-10-102-01, with 78 sites regulated by both.
source: In PS1, we thus found 234 significantly regulated sites after treatment with each of the two LRRK2 compounds GSK2578215A and HG-10-102-01 (ANOVA, p<0.005), with 78 sites regulated by both (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In PS2, 204 significantly regulated sites were identified, with 128 sites specifically downregulated in the wild type.
source: In PS2, we identified 204 significantly regulated sites (two sample t-test, FDR=0.01, S0=0.3), when comparing wild-type and inhibitor-resistant LRRK2 fibroblasts, with 128 sites specifically downregulated in the wild type, thus excluding off-target effects (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Supplementary file 3B.

claim: Rabin8 binds to the switch II domain of Rab8a and contacts the conserved, phosphorylatable T72 residue.
source: Rabin8 binds to the switch II domain of Rab8a and contacts the conserved, phosphorylatable T72 residue (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) (Guo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and a citation to Guo et al., 2013.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rab8a using LRRK2 resulted in ~60% of T72-phosphorylated protein as determined by total protein MS and LC-MS/MS after tryptic digestion.
source: To further substantiate this finding, we phosphorylated purified Rab8a using LRRK2, which resulted in ~60% of T72-phosphorylated protein as determined by total protein MS and LC-MS/MS after tryptic digestion (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: The co-crystal structure of GDI1 with the yeast Rab homologue Ypt1 shows that GDIs closely contact the switch II region.
source: The co-crystal structure of GDI1 with the yeast Rab homologue Ypt1 shows that GDIs closely contact the switch II region (Rak, 2003), which explains why phosphorylation in this domain interferes with the Rab-GDI interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rak, 2003 and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: GDIs are not specific to one Rab isoform.
source: Since GDIs are not specific to one Rab isoform (Seabra and Wasmeier, 2004), we reasoned that phosphorylation of the switch II domain could be a general mechanism of Rab-GDI dissociation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seabra and Wasmeier, 2004.

claim: Phosphorylation of the switch II domain could be a general mechanism of Rab-GDI dissociation.
source: Since GDIs are not specific to one Rab isoform (Seabra and Wasmeier, 2004), we reasoned that phosphorylation of the switch II domain could be a general mechanism of Rab-GDI dissociation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that GDIs are not specific to one Rab isoform and that phosphorylation affects GDI binding.
